newsitem.title: GERMANY: EU may return to higher land set-aside in 1997/98.
newsitem.headline: EU may return to higher land set-aside in 1997/98.

text.p: European Union farm ministers may feel compelled to raise the grain area set-aside rate for 1997/98 to limit surplus production, a German government official said on Friday.
The EU in 1996/97 halved set-aside to five percent.
"Farm council discussions on set-aside promise to be interesting...ministers may raise the rate," said Hermann Engelhardt, head of grain in the Bonn farm ministry.
Addressing a seminar during the "Green Week" farm fair, Engelhardt echoed similar remarks by state secretary Franz-Josef Feiter on Thursday, who said Germany might propose an increase.
Engelhardt said 225 million tonnes of EU grain supply from the 1996 crop and stocks compared with domestic consumption of 168-170 million tonnes.
Of the remaining 55-57 million, some 25-26 million might be exported, compared with 18 million in 1995/96.
The balance of roughly 30 million tonnes needed to be stored by traders and consumers, but around 10 million were likely to be sold into intervention.
Another 10 million tonnes might end up in intervention in 1998 as the 1997 EU crop was set to rise from 1996's 203 million tonnes due to the lower set-aside rate.
Engelhardt said Germany would argue for maintaining current EU farm policy with its in-built compensation payments until the next round of trade talks began in 1999.
Rising world grain demand might well boost global prices to levels in line with EU production costs after 2000.
But until then, the EU needed to assist its producers via set-aside, support payments and export subsidies.
